questions.q: Per this lesson, what kind of question does a governance committee exist to handle, as distinct from the day-to-day roles covered in Chapter 1?
options: Every single configuration change, no matter how small
Only questions about Salesforce licensing costs
Questions individual roles can't settle on their own -- cross-department ownership disputes, changes to the org-wide classification scheme, and approval of especially risky changes
The committee has no distinct function from the data owner role
questions.explain: The committee sits above individual roles specifically for disputes, scheme-level decisions, and high-risk approvals that a single data owner or steward can't resolve alone.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend a tiered change process rather than having the committee review every change?
options: Because committees are legally barred from reviewing more than one change per year
Because tiered processes are required by Salesforce's terms of service
Because smaller changes are never risky enough to need any review at all, under any model
Because a committee reviewing every single change, including trivial ones, becomes exactly the bottleneck governance is supposed to prevent
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly warns that committee review of every change (down to a picklist label typo) recreates the single-point-of-failure bottleneck problem from Lesson 3, just at the committee level instead of the admin level.

questions.q: In the tiered process described, what triggers a full data-governance review (classification, retention, consent, audit implications) before approval, per this lesson's examples?
options: Any change at all, including a report filter adjustment
Only changes that affect the Opportunity object
Changes are never reviewed for data-governance implications under this model
A major change such as a new integration pulling customer data into a new system, or a Data Cloud rollout unifying data across orgs
questions.explain: The lesson identifies major, high-risk changes like new integrations or a Data Cloud rollout as the tier that triggers a full data-governance review, while smaller changes get lighter or no review.

questions.q: Why does this lesson argue a governance committee staffed only by IT/the admin team is a weaker design than one with broader representation?
options: An IT-only committee systematically under-weights business risk it can't see -- a retention decision needs legal/compliance input, an ownership dispute needs someone with standing to bind both departments
IT staff are not legally permitted to sit on governance committees
Committees are required by regulation to have exactly five members
IT representatives are not capable of understanding Salesforce configuration
questions.explain: The lesson argues decisions need authority and perspective beyond IT -- legal/compliance for regulatory exposure, business operations for standing to bind departments to a resolution -- for the committee's decisions to actually carry weight.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what concrete elements does a usable escalation path to the governance committee need to define?
options: Nothing needs to be defined; escalation happens informally and is never written down
Only the committee's budget for the fiscal year
Who can bring an issue to the committee, how often it meets for routine versus urgent business, and how a decision gets communicated and recorded once made
The escalation path is identical to the Setup Audit Trail retention window
questions.explain: The lesson lists these specific elements so that a resolved dispute doesn't quietly resurface later because nobody documented how or why it was decided the first time.
